\chapter{Talking to a Friend}
\label{ch:hablas}
\hlchaptermodality{17}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what a friend does, using the tu form of an -ar verb.}

The -as ending, and the one English ending that survives beside it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hablas]{hablas — \textquotedblleft{}you speak,\textquotedblright{} to someone you know}

\label{lesson:ES-C06-hablas}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}I speak.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Hablo}.) How many words? (One.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item tú — the \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{} for a friend, a peer, someone at ease with you.
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one more letter, and it is about the other person}]
Last chapter the ending was \textbf{-o}, and it meant \emph{I}.

Swap it for \textbf{-as} and the sentence turns around to face the person you are talking to:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{hablar} $\to$ \textbf{hablas} — \emph{you speak.}
\end{quote}

Same verb. Same operation — drop the \textbf{-ar}, add an ending. Only the ending changed, and with it, who the sentence is about.

This is \emph{tú}'s form: a friend, a peer. And as before, you need no separate word for \emph{you}. \textbf{Hablas} on its own is the whole sentence.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin marked \emph{you} with \textbf{-ās}, and Spanish kept it whole: \emph{hablās} $\to$ \textbf{hablas}.

Here is the piece worth holding on to. English has almost no verb endings left — but it does have one. \textbf{He speak\emph{s}.} That lonely \textbf{-s}, the last ending standing in English, comes from the very same Latin-and-Germanic habit of putting an \emph{s} sound on a verb to mark the person.

English kept one \emph{s} and lost the rest. Spanish kept the whole set. When you learn \emph{hablas}, you are learning the system English is down to its last piece of.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hablas\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hablo\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}hablas,\textquotedblright{} and feel the sentence turn from you to the other person
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textquotedblleft{}you speak,\textquotedblright{} to a friend? (\textbf{Hablas}.) Which ending means \emph{I}, and which means \emph{you}? (\textbf{-o} and \textbf{-as}.) Which English ending is the last survivor of this system? (The \textbf{-s} in \emph{he speaks}.) Next chapter: the same verb again, for \emph{usted} — and for \emph{he} and \emph{she}.
\end{tcolorbox}
